stem: A 23-year-old woman with type I diabetes is admitted to the Emergency Department following a collapse. She tells you she has not been eating well because of nausea and vomiting and has had to reduce her insulin dose due to recurrent hypoglycaemia. Her Llying BP is 110/80 mmHg and there is a postural drop of 25mmHg on standing. explanation: Syncope, together with nausea, vomiting,hyponatraemia and borderline hyperkalaemia, is consistent with possible adrenal insufficiency. The postural drop in BP is also supportive of the diagnosis. Adrenal insufficiency, like coeliac disease, is more common in patients with type l diabetes. A short Synacthen test where adrenocorticotrophin hormone is given to stimulate endogenous cortisol release is the investigation of choice. A cortisol level of420 nmol/l at 30 minutes post-Synacthen indicates an adequate adrenal response and rules out adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal Insufficiency Media explanations.

stem: A19-year-old woman is diagnosed with cancer of the left breast. Her sister was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 26. Her father has prostate cancer and her uncle died aged 49 years from pancreatic cancer. Which mutation is most likely to be found in the family?
explanation: Both BRCA1 and BRCA2mutations are recognised to cause early-onset breast and ovarian cancers. In men, prostate cancer is seen with both BRCA1 and BRCA2mutations, but is more consistently associated with BRCA2mutations andpancreatic cancer is most strongly associated with BRCA2 mutations. Other cancers associated with BRCA2mutations include stomach, bile duct, gall bladder and melanoma. ABRCA1 BRCA1mutations are associated with early-onset breast and ovarian cancers. They are also associated with prostate cancer in men, although pancreatic cancer is more strongly associated with BRCA2. Cc-myc.

stem: A 45-year-old man with syncopal episodes is found to have heart block and is referred to the eye clinic because the doctor in the Emergency Department found limited eye movements. On further questioning,he admits to decreased night vision, such that he no longer drives at night. Which one of the following retinal findings might be related to the cardiac problem?
explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is a degenerative eye disease that can cause decreased night vision and progressive tunnel vision, due to progressive degeneration of the retinal rod cells. The combination of heart block, ocular myopathy and retinitis pigmentosa is known as Kearns-Sayre syndrome. This mitochondrial cytopathy occurs sporadically.People with this syndrome can also have ptosis, deafness,dementia and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein levels.Patients with ocular myopathy have limited eye movements but usually no diplopia because the eyes are symmetrically involved.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred to the Haematology Clinic following a routine blood test after signing on at a new General Practice. The blood film is reported as showing neutrophils which have bilobed nuclei. He is well and takes no regular medication. Physical examination is entirely normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets(PLT) 199×10/L 150-400×10/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The Pelger-Huet anomaly can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and is due to a defect in the lamin B receptor gene. Heterozygotes are clinically normal, although white cells have bilobed dumb-bell- shaped nuclei. Homozygotes do have dysfunctional neutrophils and may have an increased risk of bacterial infection. They also have increased rates of skeletal abnormalities.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with pain on intercourse, pain on passing urine and a mucopurulent discharge. She has recently split from her long-term partner. Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia is positive. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Doxycycline is the intervention of choice for treating genital chlamydia infection. It is given at a dose of 100 mg twice daily. Where it is contraindicated, then azithromycin, given at a dose of 1 g on day one and then at 500 mg on days two and three, may be the best option. Tetracyclines should not be used in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Doxycycline is preferred to azithromycin because of high rates of Mycoplasma genitalium co-infection and high rates of rectal chlamydia which is poorly cleared by azithromycin. Q.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward for NG tube feeding. Her BMI is 16 kg/m. A few hours after feeding begins, she develops hypotension and signs of left ventricular failure. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: The acute onset of hypophosphataemia can lead to the development of cardiac failure and muscle weakness. It is caused by a rapid shift of phosphate into the intracellular space as a result of hyperinsulinaemia from carbohydrate feeding. A reductionin serum potassium level is also seen. It can be avoided by ensuring adequate phosphate replacement in feeds and it is important to seek specialist Dietician advice before feeding is begun in patients with very low weight. Q.

explanation: Rifampicin is an inducer of a number of enzymes responsible for drug metabolism. These include CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9,CYP2C19 and CYP3A4.CYP3A4 is responsible for the metabolism of a number of antihypertensives and antibiotics, as well as agents such as ciclosporin used post-solid organ transplantation. explanation: This patient has Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis, as evidenced by the presence of Gram-positive diplococi. It is most likely that haematogenous spread has occurred as a result of the left-sided community- acquired pneumonia. Both vancomycin and ceftriaxone have been used as monotherapies to treat streptococcal meningitis, but combination therapy is potentially more effective. stem: A34-year-old woman is referred to the Urology Clinic with incontinence. She has given birth to her fourth child by vaginal delivery five months earlier. She says when she laughs or lifts something heavy, she loses control of her bladder. A presumptive diagnosis of stress incontinence is made. What is the fundamental feature of stress incontinence?
explanation: Increased abdominal pressure is a fundamental feature of stress incontinence. Involuntary leakage of urine is seen when total vesical pressure occurs(which includes total abdominal pressure and detrusor pressure). In classical stress incontinence, detrusor pressure should be negligible. Stress incontinence is treated in the first instance with pelvic floor exercises and weight loss for patients who are overweight or obese. Duloxetine is a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, which is licensed for the treatment of stress incontinence in patients who fail to respond to pelvic floor exercises or weight loss. stem: A 23-year-old man is admitted to the Oncology Ward for induction chemotherapy after a recent diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis against acute renal impairment?
explanation: The risk associated with induction chemotherapy for haematological malignancies is massive cell lysis, leading to a very large rise in uric acid level. Maintaining adequate hydration is key and this is often coupled with recombinant urate oxidase(rasburicase), which metabolises uric acid to allantoin and water, which are then excreted normally by the kidneys. A precipitant rise in uric acid level leads to formation of urate crystals within the renal tract and subsequent acute renal failure. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A75-year-old woman with moderate aortic stenosis is admitted to the Emergency Department with symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia. She has already had two normal colonoscopies and a normal upper GI endoscopy. She has no symptoms, apart from shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance. What is the most likely cause of this patient's iron deficiency anaemia?
options: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
explanation: Small bowel angiodysplasia is seen in association with aortic stenosis. This is known as Heyde syndrome. The location of angiodysplasia within the small bowel explains why the two colonoscopies and the upper Gl endoscopy have not identified the cause of bleeding. Capsule endoscopy can be used to confirm the diagnosis and location of chronic blood loss. Surgical resection is the definitive intervention, although embolisation or endoscopically delivered therapies may be of value in some patients. Dificulty:Average.

stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset dizziness, nausea and vomiting. He is unable to walk due to ataxia. He has nystagmus and there is loss of sensation affecting the right-hand side of his face and the left-hand side of his body. He appears to have uncontrollable hiccups. What artery is most likely to have been occluded?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with lateral medullary syndrome, which is related to vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion. Signs include those seen here,with ipsilateral sensory impairment affecting the face and contralateral symptoms affecting the body. Ataxia is caused by damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and difficulty swallowing is thought to be related to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus. Difficuty:Average.

stem: Which of the following interventions is most likely to slow deterioration in the FEVand improve the prognosis of a cigarette smoker with spirometric evidence of moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
options: Daily use of ipratropium bromide to improve FEV
Daily use of salmeterol to improve FEV
Frequent use of antibiotics for acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis
Short burst oxygen therapy at 2 L/min
explanation: There is no treatment that has been shown to significantly slow or alter the progression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) except smoking cessation. The single best thing patients with COPD can do for themselves is to stop smoking. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a common chronic respiratory illness. It is steadily progressive and carries a large burden of mortality and morbidity. It causes about 30 500 deaths per year in the UK.The morbidity burden this raises for the NHS is huge.Of all emergency medical admissions,25% are due to acute respiratory infections and COPD exacerbations comprise over half this total. The cost in hospital care for these patients is about 500 million. Housing changes and alterations add to the social costs of this disease. COPD is caused by tobacco smoking.heavy exposure to occupational dusts and chemicals, air pollution, cannabis smoking and a1-antitrypsin deficiency.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of painless intermittent diplopia which he first noticed after reading, and which worsens throughout the day. On examination the visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. There is no pupil abnormality. There is a left ptosis, partially covering the pupil, and reduced abduction and downgaze of the left eye. There are no other abnormalities on examination. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition with autoantibodies most commonly against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor on the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. It manifests as weakness or fatigability of muscles on sustained and repeated activity that improves after rest,consistent with this patient's history of worsening symptoms towards the end of the day. Ocular muscle weakness is the first presentation of myasthenia gravis in 75% of patients.Weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris causes ptosis, which is present here.The diplopia is due to weakness o the extra-ocular muscles,in this case the lateral rectus and inferior rectus,which causes an inability to abduct and depress the eye, respectively.

explanation: Bartonella henselae is responsible for cat scratch fever, which is consistent with the picture seen here. Various antibiotic options exist,including azithromycin, co-trimoxazole and ciprofloxacin.Doxycycline has historically been utilised, although response is thought to be less than that seen for macrolides.Infection is usually self-Limiting, and many patients are therefore managed without antibiotic therapy.

IVinsulin and dextrose can also be used to reduce hyperkalaemia acutely, but this takes longer to set up and to work, so calcium gluconate is normally administered immediately then followed by dextrose with or without insulin.

stem: You are treating a 56-year-old woman with angina and decide to administer isosorbide mononitrate. Which one of the following pharmacological mechanisms makes the greatest contribution to the beneficial effects of nitroglycerin?
options: Decreases oxygen transport to the myocardium
Reduces sodium-potassium transport in myocardial muscle
explanation: Nitroglycerin products are both venous capacitance dilators, and coronary and systemic artery dilators. Nitrates have complex beneficial effects on patients with coronary artery disease; they dilate systemic veins, decrease myocardial wall tension, decrease oxygen demand, cause vasodilation of large and medium-sized coronary arteries,increase coronary blood flow to the subendocardium, reduce afterload, reduced preload and increase ventricular compliance. The predominant effect of nitrates is on the venous system,reducing preload,and this myocardial oxygen demand.

Physical examination revealed white adherent patches on the oral mucosa and vagina. With respect to dosing of the drug, which of the following is the most appropriate?

Dose at 100mg three times in the week, after each dialysis session
Dose at 100mg daily but omit on dialysis days
Dose at 50mg daily for one week

explanation: Fluconazole is predominantly renally excreted, and a significant percentage of fluconazole present in plasma is removed during a 3-4h dialysis session. stem: You are asked to urgently review a54 year old woman who is 2 days post op following parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism. She is suffering from tetany affecting both wrists and pins and needles affecting both hands and the area around her mouth. When you see her she is in significant distress. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/lL 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 198×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Corrected Calcium(Ca+) 1.92 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Albumin 39 g/l 35-55 g/l Phosphate(PO-) 0.58 mmol/l 0.70-1.40 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The postoperative hypocalcemia is probably due to acute reversal of previously elevated PTH levels.In the high turnover state associated with hyperparathyroidism,PTHincreases bone formaion and resorption with a ne eflux of calcium from bone. Sudden withdrawal of PTHin such patients leads to an acute imbalance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity. causing a marked net increase in bone uptake of calcium. phosphate and magnesium.IV calcium is essential in the acute management of a patient with tetany, as in this case.Magnesium should also be measured as hypomagnesaemia is common and replacement is likely to be needed.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations and pre-syncope. She tells you that the palpitations began whilst she was driving to work. She had drunk a large amount of alcohol the previous evening at a hen party, and followed this up with caffeine in the morning to enable her to get up for work. On examination, her BP is 110/80 mmHg with pulse 180 bpm. She is not in cardiac failure. ECG reveals a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia of 180 bpm. Venous blood gases reveal a potassium of 4.1 mmol/L. Which of the following is the next most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Both excess alcohol consumption and caffeine are recognised as risk factors for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia(SVT), and it is likely that combination has driven the episode of tachycardia. Carotid sinus massage is a reasonable first step in attempting conversion to sinus rhythm, and can be attempted whilst the adenosine is being drawn up.

stem: An 18-year-old student is admitted to the Emergency Department after suffering a fit following a night out at the pub. His friends heard him having a seizure and called an ambulance. explanation: In this situation, with likely chronic hypoglycaemia, low muscle and liver glycogen reserve is a possibility. This means that when alcohol related hypoglycaemia occurs,in spite of a counter-regulatory hormone response, there is limited mobilisation of stored carbohydrate,leading to significant,symptomatic, hypoglycaemia.This patient must be encouraged to eat after alcohol and if possible step back on his insulin to maintain a slightly higher HbA1c.

stem: An 85-year-old woman is in a nursing home and has mild Alzheimer's disease. She has ischaemic heart disease with occasional angina on exertion but is otherwise well. Her GP refers her to Haematology Outpatients because of a persistently raised white cell count. When she is seen she has no complaints and there is nothing abnormal to find on examination. Her full blood picture is as follows: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 114 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 27×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 140×10/L 150-400×10/L Neutrophils 3.6×10/L 2.5-7.58×10/L Lymphocytes 21.9×10/L 1.5-3.5×10/L Monocytes 1.5×10/L 0-0.8×10/L Smear cells reported as seen on the film. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her raised white cell count?
explanation: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is the correct answer in this very elderly lady with a raised white cell count and a raised lymphocyte count.Smear cells are reported on the blood film.This is an atypical presentation of CLL, ie identified as an incidental finding when blood tests are performed for other reasons. Cell urface markers,also known as flow cytometry or immunophenotyping,should be performed to establish the nature of the lymphocytes.

stem: A 63-year-old man with a history of Type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He complains of a dull ache in his left thigh over the past few weeks, and numbness over the medial side of the leg. Apparently his leg has also given way and buckled whilst he was climbing the stairs on 2-3 occasions. His diabetes is poorly controlled on 3 oral medications;he refuses insulin therapy and a recent HbA1c was raised at76 mmol/mol(9.1%). Examination reveals weakness and wasting of the quadriceps muscle on the left hand side. There is loss of sensation confirmed on the medial side of the thigh. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Diabetic femoral neuropathy is well recognised in patients with long-standing diabetes. Abnormal femoral nerve conduction is found in a high percentage of patients with diabetes mellitus, even those with no femoral nerve symptoms.Clinical femoral neuropathy is thought to be related to an inflammatory vasculitis and is seen more commonly in patients who experience extremes of glycaemic control. Physiotherapy to maintain muscle strength is the mainstay of treatment for diabetic femoral neuropathy.

stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the Urology Assessment Clinic for review. She is referred by her GP because of urge incontinence, she says that she can hardly make it to the toilet to empty her bladder, and is incontinent of urine up to 2-3 times per week. She drinks 5 cups of strong coffee per day. There is no past medical history of note. Her BP is 122/82;pulse is 70 and regular. BMl is 25.Urine analysis is normal, and renal function is also within the normal range. Which of the following initial treatments is most appropriate?
explanation: This patient appears to have mainly urge incontinence symptoms for which reducing caffeine intake would be a logical first option.In addition she should be encouraged to regularise her overall daily fluid intake, especiallyif there are large changes from day to day.Muscarinic receptor antagonists are a logical next step.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with low mood. He has felt depressed all his life and never feels good for more than a week, but has never had suicidal or psychotic episodes and has been able to continue work despite his depression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dysthymia is the persistent(2 years)symptoms of chronic low-grade depression; however, the symptoms of dysthymia do not meet the full criteria for a diagnosis of major depression. It usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood and patients tend to have low mood, brood, sleep badly and feel inadequate, but are able to cope with the demands of daily Life. Treatment with antidepressants or cognitive behavioural therapy may be helpful in severe cases.

stem: You review a 68-year-old man with cancer and severe anxiety. He is not keen to have surgical intervention and wants to consider radiotherapy. For which one of the following tumours is radiotherapy most commonly used as a curative intervention?
explanation: Radiotherapy may be curative in certain types of retinal, CNS,skin, oropharynx, larynx,oesophageal, cervical,vaginal and prostatic tumours.It may also be curative when used as the sole treatment for certain types of lymphoma. Radiotherapy can be curative when used as an adjuvant to primary surgery for lung,breast, uterine,bladder, rectal, seminomatous and sarcomatous tumours.Radiotherapy is not used curatively in the management of colonic(excluding rectal) or gastric carcinoma. The palliative benefits of radiotherapy include pain relief, relief of headache and vomiting when used for CNS tumours, relief of GI, bladder or lymphatic obstruction, preservation of skeletal integrity from bony metastases, and temporary reverse of neurological impairment associated with spinal cord impingement.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic as a new patient. He has just moved to the area and so wishes to move his care to your hospital-he has previously been under follow up in a respiratory clinic elsewhere for bronchiectasis. Unfortunately, his old clinic has not yet provided you with his past history. He tells you that 2 years ago he received treatment for a lung infection 'that was like tuberculosis, but not'.You assume he had some sort of atypical mycobacterial infection. Which one of the following is the most likely organism to have caused respiratory disease in this setting?
explanation: The atypical mycobacteria are environmental mycobacterial species that do not cause tuberculosis or leprosy. MAC is probably the most important in the UK, where it can cause respiratory disease(in the immunosuppressed, or also in the immunocompetent-generally those with a pre-existing lung condition, as in this patient) or disseminated disease (usually only seen in advanced HIV).

stem: A 17-year-old man with a history of epilepsy comes to the Emergency Department having suffered a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He is currently taking dual anti-epileptic drug therapy, and suffers 1-2 seizures per month. There is a past history of learning difficulties, although he does manage to hold down a job in a café for 3 days per week. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. He is post ictal with a GCS of 13.You notice a number of small reddish nodules affecting the skin folds on either side of the nose, which have coalesced to form larger nodular lesions in certain areas. On general examination you notice that he has a number of skin tags, areas of depigmentation on his torso, and has ungual fibromas affecting the nails on both hands. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his epilepsy?
explanation: The facial appearance is suggestive of adenoma sebaceum, with skin tags and ungual fibromas and ash leaf macules all pointing towards an underlying diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis.Hamartoma formation in the brain from an early age is associated with the development of epilepsy.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a known history of alcoholic cirrhosis presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. He has suffered from increasing oedema affecting both lower limbs and ascites over the past few weeks.On examination his BP is 112/82 mmHg; pulse is 78/min and regular.There are multiple spider naevi over the upper chest, moderate ascites and bilateral pitting oedema affecting to below the knee. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/L 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 95×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 132 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 80 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 22 g/l 35-55 g/l Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 152 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline Phosphatase 210 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Which of the following is the most useful diuretic in this situation?
explanation: Hyperaldosteronism has a major role in the development of ascites in patients with liver failure. Splanchnic vasodilatation leads to compensatory activation of the renin angiotensin system and consequent elevation of aldosterone. In addition, metabolism of steroid hormones such as aldosterone is reduced in liver failure, leading to further worsening of ascites.

stem: A51-year-old male from West Africa comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review.He has a number of well- demarcated areas of depigmented skin affecting both his arms and legs and his lower abdomen. When you examine him, sensation over these depigmented lesions is found to be significantly decreased; in addition, there is thickening of underlying peripheral nerves when you examine the lesions on his arms and legs.He has lost a few kilograms in weight recently and feels generally lethargic but has no other significant symptoms. nvestigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/L 135-175g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 10.4×10/L 4-11×10/ Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 110μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 65 mm/15th 0-10 mm in the 1thour C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 82 mg/L 0-10 mg/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The elevated inflammatory markers, coupled with well-demarcated, depigmented, areas of skin with loss of sensation,are consistent with a diagnosisof leprosy.The thickening of underlying peripheral nerves 5upports the diagnosis even further.The gold standard for diagnosis is slit-skin biopsy to confirm the presence of Mycobacterium leprae. For tuberouloid leprosy treatment with a two-drug regimen (rfampicin and dapsone) is recommended fo a period of 6 months.Triple therapy rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine) is recommended for lepromatous leprosy.in which lesions are more extensive and eye and lung signs are also present.

stem: A 21-year-old female student who is taking the contraceptive pill presents with a short history of dysuria. She has just completed a year abroad in France and tells you she has had four new sexual partners during this time. On examination she has multiple, shallow and tender ulcers at the skin and mucous membrane of the vagina. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 or 2.Genital herpes classically presents with multiple painful ulcers, which can cause significant dysuria and in extreme cases, urinary retention. Primary infection is usually the most severe, and can also present with general systemic upset.The herpes virus then becomes latent, and can recur-however,generally with less severe symptoms than the primary infection. References: British Association for Sexual Healt &HIV. UK national guideline for the management of anogenital herpes Macclesfield:BASHH,2014.

stem: An 18-year-old student is referred to the Neurology Clinic for review. He suffers from excessive daytime sleepiness such that he is often unable to keep awake in lessons. He also suffers periods of collapse caused by generalised muscle weakness, during which he says consciousness is preserved.These are brought on by periods of emotion such as laughing, anger, or upset. According to his parents who attend the appointment with him, he also has problems with sleep walking. On examination his BP is 110/80 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. BMI is 21.Neurological examination is entirely normal. Routine blood testing is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the epsiodes of collapse?
explanation: The episodes of collapse are highly suggestive of episodes of cataplexy. particularly as the weakness occurs during periods of high emotion and consciousness is preserved through out.Excessive daytime sleepiness in the absence of risk factors for obstructive sleep apnoea further supports the diagnosis.Modafinil is the intervention of choice for predominant daytime sleepiness. with respect to cataplexy episodes, evidence supports the use SSRls or SNRIs such as Fluoxetine or Venlafaxine.

stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the Renal Clinic for review. He undergoes haemodialysis three times per week for renal failure related to diabetes mellitus, has suffered from 3 previous Mls over the past 5 years and most recently had two TIAs over the last 3 months. He takes multiple medications including calcium and vitamin D,and follows a low phosphate diet. His main complaint is of bony aches and pains. On examination his BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 80 bpm and regular. His BMl is 23.There is evidence of proximal myopathy when you ask him to stand from a low chair in the clinic. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/lL 135-175 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 7.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 355μmol/L 50-120μmol/L Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 3.1 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/l Phosphate(PO) 1.5 mmol/L 0.70-1.40 mmol/l Alkaline Phosphatase 182 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Parathyroid hormone(PTH) 14.0(ULN 6.8) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: explanasticns Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic, which mimics the action of calcium on the calcium sensing receptor.In this case.

stem: A 72-year-old man who is maintained on long-term warfarin therapy is referred to the anti-coagulation clinic because his warfarin requirements have decreased by approximately 50%. He has started a long-term course of metronidazole a few days earlier for a dental abscess. Inhibition of which of the following p450 enzymes is responsible for the decreased warfarin requirements?
explanation: Warfarin is a mixture of R-and S-enantiomers that are metabolised by different CYPP450 cytochromes.R- warfarin is metabolised primarily by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4,and S-warfarin is metabolised primarily by CYP2C9.Metronidazole is an inhibitor of 2C9,3A4 and 3A5-7;2C9 inhibition causes animportant interaction with the S-enantiomer, which is the one that confers greatest clinical efficacy. A1A2 1A2 is incorrect.Drugs that interfere with CYP1A2 may influence warfarin effects but the key interaction with metronidazole is its inhibitory effects on other isoenzymes.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic by her GP.She has thickening of the skin over the fingers of both hands, and around her mouth, and a number of telangiectasiae. She also has flitting joint pains affecting multiple small joints and says that her fingers are extremely painful in cold weather. She takes Indapamide for hypertension but is otherwise well. On examination his BP is 139/89 mmHg;pulse is 80/min and regular. There is obvious tight skin around her mouth with multiple telangiectasiae over the face. There is peripheral calcinosis and scleroderma. Chest is clear. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115-155g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 6.0×109/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 188×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 4.5 mmol/L 3.9-7.1 mmol/L Anti-nuclear Antibody positive Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate(ESR) 55 mm/1sthour 0-10 mm in the 15thour Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be found?
explanation: This patient has evidence of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, which is most strongly associated with anti-centromere antibodies. Patients who are ani-centromere positive are relatively protected from lung fibrosis, although the antibody is associated with increased risk of pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 32-year-old man is referred to the Hypertension Clinic for review. His GP is concerned about his BP,which is still elevated at 170/95mmHg, despite having recently started Amlodipine 5mg daily, and he is suffering from persistent morning headaches. There is no other past medical history of note. On examination in the clinic BP is confirmed at 175/95 mmHg,pulse is 80/min and regular. His BMl is 23. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 105μmol/L 50-120 mmol/L Glucose 4.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Abdominal USS Right adrenal mass Which of the following anti-hypertensives is likely to be most effective in controlling his BP?
explanation: Given the marked hypokalaemia and adrenal mass,hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism is the most likely underlying diagnosis.In this situation giving an aldosterone antagonist such as Spironolactone is the most appropriate intervention with respect to reduction of BP. If there is a concern about gynaecomastia or breast tenderness, then Eplerenone may be considered as an alternative.

stem: A 24-year-old student nurse presents to the clinic for review. She has suffered increasing episodes of collapse over the past 6months, including some whilst on attachment, and gradual weight gain. She tells you that she feels tired nearly every morning and worries there is a serious problem with her health. One sample collected during a collapse in the Emergency Department reveals a c-peptide of 0.2 nmol/L(normal range:0.51 to 2.72 ng/mL), glucose of 1.9 mmol/L,and elevatedinsulin. She has no past medical history of note and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. Examination reveals a BP of 135/85mmHg;pulse is 65/min and regular. Her BMI is 26. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged The major pointer here is the fact the insulin is elevated and the c-peptide low at 0.2 nmoll during a proven episode of hypoglycaemia.In this situation the differential between c-peptide and insulin means that exogenous insulin administration is the only possibility. Confirming the diagnosis is dificut,with confrontation often resuting in straight denial, a prolonged period of counselling is usually required.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with right iliac fossa pain, a fever and vomiting. She has just returned from a holiday in Spain where she had unprotected sexual intercourse with three partners over the course of the week. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill but uses no other regular medication. On examination her BP is 105/70 mmHg;pulse is 90/min and regular.Her temperature is 38.5℃. She has signs of peritonism and is particularly tender in the right iliac fossa.PR reveals an empty rectum. Investigations; nvestigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 15.1×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/ C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 245mg/l 0-10 mg/l Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 142μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine blood 1+ Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In this situation the diagnosis to exclude is appendicitis, and abdominal USS is the logical first step in a5sessment A healthy appendix is not normally visible on USS,although in appendicitis USS demonstrates a tubular structure 7-9mm in diameter that is non-compressible. In conjunction with other markers such as raised WCC and CRP,it can guide progression to surgery.

stem: A 23-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is suffering from pain at the base of both thumbs that she attributes to lifting her first child, who is 9 months old. On examination, there is thickening over the radial styloid on both wrists.Both flexion of the thumb and ulnar deviation at the wrist are demonstrated to reproduce the pain. No other abnormalities are identified clinically. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis are tightly secured against the radial styloid by the overlying extensor retinaculum.Thickening of the tendons from acute or repetitive trauma prevents the tendons from gliding easily through the sheath, leading to further inflammation. Efforts at thumb motion, especially when combined with radial or ulnar deviation of the wrist, cause pain. Rest and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the initial mainstay of therapy, with surgical decompression being the next step.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with malaise, nausea and vomiting, particularly in the mornings, and frontal headaches over the past 3 months. She is sexually active but feels she has lost her Libido and has not had a period since these symptoms began. She takes no regular medications. Examination reveals a BP of 105/80 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. BMI is 25.Visual fields are normal. Investigations; nvestigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 115g/l 115-155g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 204×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 24 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline Phosphatase 162 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 12μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Glucose 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L* Prolactin 1865 mU/L 400 mU/L Oestrogen 800 pmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Given this patient's age and the fact she is sexually active,morning sickness coupled with elevated oestrogen and prolactin in the presence of amenorrhoea, fits with a diagnosis of pregnancy until proven otherwise.The next togical step is therefore a urine pregnancy test.

stem: A 42-year-old man attends the Infertility Clinic as a new referral from his GP. His sperm count is noted to be low, and the GP suspects that he has a left varicocele. Other history of note includes hypertension,for which he takes ramipril, and night sweats intermittently over the past few months. ESR is markedly raised and anaemia is noted on full blood count. Urinalysis reveals the presence of haematuria. What diagnosis may best explain this clinical conundrum?
explanation: Renal-cell carcinoma may rarely present with a left-sided varicocele, due to tumour invasion of the left renal vein, interfering with drainage from the left testicular vein. Patients with renal-cell carcinoma often present with haematuria,associated loin pain and a flank mass.Malaise,anorexia and weight loss are said to occur in around 30% of patients, and 5% of patients may present with polycythaemia. However,various abnormal haematological patterns may be seen,including anaemia,raised ESR and coagulation abnormalities.Pyrexia occurs in around 20% and around one-quarter of patients have metastases at the time of diagnosis. The tumours may be solitary, multiple or occasionally bilateral.Tumours originate within the kidney but may eventually penetrate the renal capsule.Macroscopically,they appear as a yellow mass, sometimes containing areas of haemorrhage and cystic degeneration.Prognosis depends on the tumour stage at diagnosis:the 5-year survival rate is 60-70% with tumours confined to the renal parenchyma; 15-35% where there is lymph node involvement and only 5% in patients with distant metastases.

stem: A 17-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with tiredness, lethargy and facial oedema. He has history of two previous episodes of nephrotic syndrome, which resolved following a 6 week course of oral Prednisolone. On examination his BP is elevated at 155/85mmHg,pulse is 78/min and regular.There is obvious periorbital oedema, and bilateral pitting oedema of the lower limbs. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 120 g/L 135-175 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 8.9×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 173×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 108μmol/L 50-120μmol/L Albumin 23 g/l 35-55 g/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 35 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline Phosphatase 89 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Urine protein +++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The repeated episodes in chitdhood, coupled with raid response to steroids.suggest that minimal change disease is the most likely cause of the nephrotic syndrome seen here. Corticosteroids are the mainstay of therapy in adults and children; although more prolonged treatment may be needed to gain a response in aduts. Ciclosporin is commonly used in patients who fail to respond to coticosteroids alone.

stem: You are evaluating the QT effect of a new agent for the treatment of depression. Which of the following correctly describes the way to measure the QT interval?
options: Beginning of the Q wave to end of the T wave
End of the Q wave to end of the T wave
End of the Q wave to beginning of the T wave
End of the Q wave to mid-point of the T wave
Mid-point of the Q wave to the beginning of the T wave
explanation: Most ECG machines are now automated and no actual measurement on the part of the operator is required. Heart rate significantly impacts on interpretation of QT interval, for this reason values corrected for heart rate are usually quoted.Two formulae exist,QTcF,and QTcB, for the purposes of clinical trials the F adjustment is preferred because it is more accurate at high and low heart rates.

stem: A 22-year-old patient with testicular feminisation comes to the clinic for review. What would you expect the patient's phenotype to be?
options: Female with normal genitalia but no pubic or axillary hair
Female with normal genitalia and short stature
Male with normal testicular size and body hair
Male with small testicular size and sparse body hair
explanation: Patients with androgen insensitvity syndrome(AIS) have no pubic and axillary hair,and scanty hair on the rest of the body. They do not have acne and breast developmentis normal because of conversion of testosterone to oestrodiol. Incidence of bilateral inguinal herniae is increased in childhood in patients with AIS, and undescended testes are identified at this stage. Patients with AIS are infertile.

stem: You are asked to review a 70-year-old man on the Coronary Care Unit who is 3h post-percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for an anterolateral myocardial infarction. He has maintained his BP at 122/82 mmHg post-procedure, but the nurses are concerned as his pulse rate has increased to 108/min and the complexes have broadened on the monitor. He is not in cardiac failure. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The most likely cause of the changes seen on the monitor is bundle branch block related to the infarct.The ventricular rate, the fact he has no ongoing chest pain and that he is not in cardiac failure all count against a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia(VT).

stem: You want to know the strength of the correlation between weight and blood pressure in the population of patients admitted to the Emergency Department of the hospital over the past 6 months. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to analyse the relationship between the two variables?
explanation: Pearson's correlation coefficient is the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations. It has a value between 1 and-1 and indicates whether there is a positive or negative relationship between two variables.A value 0.5 would be considered a very strong correlation between weight and BP.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a bipolar disorder has been prescribed lithium. Which of the following pharmacological features should best be kept in mind when prescribing this drug?
options: Amiloride is a specific antidote for lithium toxicity
Lithium may cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Serum lithium level should not exceed 2 mmol/L
explanation: Long-term treatment with lithium causesinsensitivity of ADH receptors causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.It is aso associated with progressive chronic kidney disease.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents via his GP for assessment. He has lost 2 stone in weight over the past 4 months without trying, and has persistent iron deficiency anaemia that has not improved with iron supplementation. He has no history of indigestion and no significant change in bowel habit. A past history of asthma for which he takes a Salbutamol inhaler is noted. He drinks 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination his BP is 135/82 mmHg;pulse is 70 and regular. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear. Abdomen is soft and non- tender, and BMI is 23.PR reveals an empty rectum with no masses. nvestigations; nvestigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101g/l 135-175 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume(MCV) 77 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×109/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Faecal occult blood positive Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In this situation with no specific symptoms apart from weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia, the possibility of a right-sided colonic tumour is raised.As such the optimal way to image it is via a coonoscopy. Adequate prep is essential, and if optimal views are not obtained, either a repeat or a CT colonoscopy would be advised.

stem: A75-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion and a fall. He has been admitted 3 times with a urinary tract infection over the past 6months. Other past medical history of note includes hypertension and diabetes mellitus for which he takes a number of medications including Metformin, Sitagliptin, Ramipril and Simvastatin.On examination his BP is 110/80 mmHg; pulse is 90/min and regular. He is pyrexial 38.8℃ and tender over his lower abdomen. Whilst you are examining him he lashes out at you and digs his nails into your arm, and then tries to get up off the bed but slips onto the floor.
explanation: In this situation with acute confusion and aggression as a result of urinary tract infection,NICE guidance recommends the use of either Haloperidol or Lorazepam.A small starting dose such as0.5mg is most appropiate and can be given IMor IV if the patient is non-cD-operative with oral medication. In patients with significant Parkinsonism, Lorazepam is preferred to Haloperidol.

stem: A35-year-old man with a history of Type 1 diabetes for 30 years comes to the clinic for review. He is currently managed with a basal bolus insulin regime, has up to 20 serious hypoglycaemic episodes per year, and his most recent HbA1cwas 55mmol/mol(7.2%). He is not currently taking any medication apart from insulin. On examination his BP is 125/85mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 24.There is loss of fine touch and proprioception affecting both feet Investigations; nvestigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.9×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets 182×10/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 122μmol/L 50-120μmol/L HbA1c 55 mmol/mol(7.2%) 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) Urine protein ++(urinary protein 1.3g/24hr) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to delay progression of renal disease?
explanation: Increased insulin dose is incorrect. Increased insulin dose is ill advised in this situation given that HbA1cis near target at 7.2% and the patient is already having a number of serious hypos per year.Although some benefit might be derived by achieving hbA1c below 7%, the impact will not be as great as that achieved by ACE inhibition.

stem: A47-year-old shopkeeper who has been on analgesics for rheumatoid arthritis for the past 2 years now complains of increasing pain, stiffness and swelling in his finger joints. Which radiological feature would be most suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Punched out erosions in juxta-articular bone
explanation: Periarticular osteoporosis is a characteristic X-ray finding in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A32-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with his 28-year-old wife who is brought in by ambulance. His wife had been behaving strangely, almost hyperactive during the previous 2 days, but has now become drowsy, confused and forgetful. Her only medication of note is the oral contraceptive pill. She is confused and drowsy,her temperature is 37.9℃ and her BP is 155/85 mmHg, you note a cold sore on her upper lip. Fundoscopy is normal, there is mild meningism,and GCS is reduced at 13. Investigations; nvestigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 128 g/L 135-175g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 10.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 128 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive protein (CRP) 45 mg/l 0-10 mg/l areas of low density affecting the anterior CT head and medial portions of the temporal lobes, more marked on the left Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Clues here include the confusion with a modest rise in CRP,hyponatraemia and temporal lobe changes on the CT head. Coupled with the cold sore,they raise the possibility of herpes simplex encephalitis. In this situation IVAciclovir should not be delayed,and lumbar puncture with PCR for HSV is a key stepin confirming the diagnosis.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He complains of posterior neck pain, has reduced sensation below his upper chest and is unable to move his arms and legs. On examination BP is mildly elevated at 145/90 mmHg, with a pulse of 85/min. Pain and temperature sensation is reduced below the upper chest, although proprioception and vibration sense is retained. Power in the upper and lower limbs is 0/5(MRC grading), and reflexes are absent throughout the limbs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dimieulty Average Pcer Responses %6 Quadriplegia, with pain and temperature sensory loss but preservation of vibration sense and proprioception is typical of anterior spinal artery syndrome The anterior spinal cord contains the corticospinal tracts [motor function) andthe spinothalamic tracts (pain and temperature sensation).hence the loss of these functions. However, vibration and proprioceptive sensation travels in the dorsal columns (posterior cordj:consequently these functions are spared in an anterior cord syndrome.This patient's anterior cord syndrome is most likely caused by trauma as a result of the accident He is complaining of posterior neck pain and loss of sensation from the upper chest,and therefore the lesion is likely to be cervical.MRl is the investigation of choice to confirm the likely aetiology Unfortunately prognosis is very poor, and mortality is as high as 20%.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is enrolled on a methadone program for withdrawal of heroin. She is into the first week of the program when she has a sudden collapse whilst walking in the street. Unfortunately resuscitation by paramedics at the scene is unsuccessful. At a coroners'inquest it transpires there is a family history of sudden death, with 3 members of the immediate family having died aged under 40 years. Which of the following is the most likely cause of sudden death in the family?
explanation: Methadone is well known to lead to QT prolongation. In a patient with a family history of sudden death, the most likely underlying cause is therefore congenital long QT syndrome. Episodes of VT occur more frequently in patients with long QT when there is underlying sympathetic activation, either through exercise or emotional stress. Beta blockade is therefore the initial therapy of choice.QT prolonging drugs such as methadone should of course be avoided at all costs.

stem: A54-year-old man with a known history of cirrhosis related to alcohol consumption is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward. He has felt increasingly lethargic over the past few days and a rise in his creatinine from 85μmol/l to 115μmol/L, coupled with a decrease in urine output is noted. Despite stopping his diuretics, the fall-off in urne output persists. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135-175 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×109/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 102×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 133 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 115μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 115 IU/L 5-30 IU/L
explanation: Splanchnic vasodilatation is thought to lie at the heart of hepatorenal syndrome, where despite intense renal artery vasoconstriction. there is a worsening in renal perfusion and a consequent rise in creatinine. Tertipressin,which leads to splanchnic vasoconstriction, is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 23-year-old student presents two months after a trip to Thailand feeling generally unwell. He admits to multiple sexual partners while abroad. On examination he has a temperature of 37.4,a blood pressure of 122/70 and a heart rate of 90.His chest is clear with normal heart sounds, however he has a generalised skin rash, painless lymphadenopathy and oral ulceration. Investigations: HIV indeterminate VDRL positive TPHA positive HBsAg neg HBeAg neg HBsAb positive Which one of the following options is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The presentation with systemic upset,rash,lymphadenopathy and oral ulceration 'snail-track ulcers') would be consistent with secondary syphilis, with occurs one to six months after initial infection.Serological testing for syphilis is split into two types: Syphils explanations 1. Non-treponeme specific (VDRL, RPR) – positive in active disease, negative after successful treatment or in Late disease. Can be positive in range of other conditions including pregnancy.SLE, TB etc 2. Treponeme specific (TPHA, FTA) – positive in active disease, and remains so following treatment. Also positive in other related treponeme disease – e.g. yaws. This case has a positive VDRL and a positive TPHA.which would be consistent with active syphilis.

stem: A41-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after a collapse whilst chasing a shoplifter down the street. He admits to a splitting headache and tachycardia at the time of the chase. On further questioning it transpires that he has suffered from increasing headaches, particularly in the mornings, over the past few months. On examination his BP is 155/94 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There are no murmurs and his chest is clear. His BMI is 23.Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations; nvestigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131g/L 135-175 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×109/L 150-400×109/ Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 7.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L USS Evidence of left adrenal mass Which of the following is the optimal way to control his BP?
explanation: Phenoxybenzamine is a non-selective alpha antagonist,which is the anti-hypertensive of choice in the treatment of phaeochromocytoma,the most likely diagnosis here. The starting dose is 10mg pe day and this may be increased at 10mg /day until BPis controlled.Other alpha-blockers such as Doxazosin are shorter acting and may result in rebound hypertension.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is reviewed in the Outpatient Department some 6 weeks after discharge following an episode of severe gram-negative sepsis. She had a short period on the High Dependency Unit for which she required therapy with a number of antibiotics including an aminoglycoside. She is concerned as her family tell her she has problems with her hearing. In addition she has suffered a rise in her creatinine from 115 micromol/l checked at her GP's some 3 months ago,to 149 micromol/l now. Which of the following is the mechanism that drives Gentamicin nephrotoxicity?
explanation: Gentamicin is endocytosed by megalin, a transmembrane protein found in proximal tubule cells, after binding to their phospholipid membrane.Gentamicin then travels via the Golgi complex to the cytosol,from whence it accumulates in mitochondria and the nucleus.It interferes with protein sorting and synthesis,which leads to nephrotoxicity. The mechanism of ototoxicity is less clear,athough it appears to be associated with a sustained time above recommended peak concentration and may be related to positive modulation of NMDA receptors.

stem: A 42-year-old cotton worker from Southern India is staying with her brother in London. While here, they pay for a private medical consultation. She reports what sounds like a work-related illness. During the first hour at work after the weekend she reports severe shortness of breath, cough and chest tightness; this appears to ease gradually during the week, only to return after the next weekend off. Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
explanation: Byssinosis is now rare in the UK as the number of cotton mills has declined, but it still occurs in areas of cotton production, such as in India. It is characteristically associated with symptoms of shortness of breath, cough and chesttightness that begin on the first day of the working week and ease during the remainder of the working week. It is thought to be due to endotoxin released by bacteria that are found in cotton dust. There are usually no demonstrable chestX-ray changes.It is thought that the more severe changes noted in some patients might be related to associated asthma or cigarette smoking.

stem: A 22-year-old man, who has recently been circumcised, presents with pruritic purple papules on the scar and on his ankles. These are covered in fine white scale. Oral examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: · Classicat lichen planus is characterised by an itchy, violaceous,polygonal, flat-topped papular rash most commonly developing over the wrists and ankles. ·A pale, lacy network is often-but not always-found in the mouth,athough this may be asymptomatic. ·The presence of Wickham's striae-afine, white lacy pattern over the papules-is characteristic. ·The Koebner phenomenon is typically seen in lichen planus (whereby the rash 'colonises'sites of trauma a few days later). · It has been associated with liver disease including heptitis C., primary biliary cholangitis and chronic active hepatitis,although this is unlikely to be a consideration in this case. ·It usually resolvesin 6-18 months. ·Lichen planus often responds to potent o very potent topical steroid,but some patients willrequire oral prednisolone.

stem: You are examining expression of genes that could be linked to a proximal muscle wasting disorder. Which of the following fits best with regards to the human genome?
options: Mitochondrial disorders follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern
Only 50% of the human genome is comprised of non-coding DNA
Zinc finger nucleases are the best way to edit the genome
explanation: DNA methylation at the 5 position of cytosine has the specific effect of reducing gene expression. Methylation is recognised to be responsible for a number of diseases affected by the interaction between the organism and the environment including metabolic disorders and cancer.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with an itchy scaling rash affecting his scalp and the folds of skin around his nose. He tells you that he has had problems with flaky skin and dandruff for years, but now wants it sorted out. He has no other medical problems, smokes 5 cigarettes per day and drinks 10 pints of beer per week. On examination there is a scaling rash affecting the scalp with areas of erythema and extensive dandruff. A similar erythematous rash is seen affecting the naso-labial folds and is found behind the ears. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: The clinical picture described here fits best with a diagnosis of seborrheic dermatitis.In this situation a 2% Ketoconazole preparation, as a shampoo for the scalp, and as cream for the nasal folds has been shown to significantly reduce symptoms and is the initial treatment of choice. Selenium based shampoos can be considered as an alternative.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with manic depressive psychosis, obesity and hypertension comes to the clinic. Her GP is unsure of the optimal way to manage her blood pressure. On examination in the clinic her BP is 155/95 mmHg, with pulse 78/min and regular. Her body mass index(BMI) is 36.Investigations reveal a fasting glucose of 6.3 mmol/L. Which of the following is the optimal way to treat her hypertension, bearing in mind she takes lithium?
explanation: Prescribing anti-hypertensives in conjunction with lithium therapy is dificult as a number of agents increase the risk of toxicity.These include thiazides, angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers.This leaves us with the option of using either a beta blocker or the dihydropyridine calcium antagonist. Out of the two,beta blockers are known to worsen glucose intolerance and, given that her BMl is very elevated and she has impaired fasting glucose,atenolol is therefore not the favoured option. This leaves felodipine as the favoured option for treating her blood pressure.

stem: A19-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following a third episode of meningococcal meningitis in the last four years. Which of the following deficiencies is the most likely cause?
explanation: C5, along with components 6-9 of the complement system, are the components of the membrane attack complex. Deficiency of these factors increases the risk of bacterial infection, with Neisseria meningitidis in particular. C5 deficiency is also associated with wasting, chronic diarrhoea and widespread seborrhoeic dermatitis in children, a condition known as Leiner's disease.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has bronchiectasis. She suffers from recurrent haemoptysis and wants to know why this is occurring. Which of the following fits best with the pathophysiology of haemoptysis in bronchiectasis?
explanation: Capillary engorgement is a feature of bronchiectasis and is associated with chronic infection in the condition. It is also seen in tuberculosis and cystic fibrosis. Erosion and potential rupture of the pulmonary capillaries or adjacent bronchial arteries are seen and it is this that results in haemoptysis. If a large vessel is eroded, then haemoptysis can be massive. Embolisation may be required in the acute situation in the event of massive pulmonary haemorrhage.

stem: A72-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review following a left Colles' fracture. She is to be treated with risedronate, a bisphosphonate taken monthly. What is the most important risk factor for osteonecrosis of the jaw as a result of bisphosphonate treatment?
explanation: Dental caries is the strongest risk factor for osteonecrosis of the jaw. If bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy is considered, then patients should be referred to the dentist and any work carried out before the first dose is given. Other risk factors for osteonecrosis of the jaw include smoking, age65 years and long-term use of corticosteroids. Advanced osteonecrosis of the jaw requires debridement, whereas relatively minor disease can initially be managed with mouthwash and antibiotics.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with breast cancer comes to the Palliative Care Clinic for review of her pain relief. She is currently taking short-acting morphine up to six times per day. Her average dose over the past week has been 120 mg of morphine per day. What is the most appropriate initial dose of morphine slow-release tablets?
explanation: This patientis using an average of 120 mg of standard-release morphine per day. Modified-release morphine preparations are given twice a day, meaning that this is divided by two and given as a 60-mg twice-a-day dose. The patient should retain access to Oramorph, so that they can use it for breakthrough pain.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is assessed one week following a stroke which led to dysphasia and weakness affecting her left side. What is the most useful score for assessing this patient's independence?
explanation: The Barthel Index is used post-stroke to determine the level of independence and likely long-term care needs. It includes measures of continence, personal grooming, toilet use, feeding, transferring, mobility, dressing, stairs and bathing. Scores of 0-20 indicate full dependency, 21-60 severe dependency, 61-90 moderate dependency and 91-99 slight dependency.

stem: A 39-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a third episode of renal colic in the past nine months, despite increasing his fluid intake and reducing carbonated drinks.The cause has been identified as calcium oxalate stones. What is the most appropriate prophylaxis against further episodes of renal colic?
explanation: Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide and bendroflumethiazide, reduce urinary calcium excretion and can be used as prophylaxis in patients who suffer from recurrent calcium oxalate urinary stones. As well as using thiazides, patients should be encouraged to restrict their salt intake to6 g/day.

stem: A 67-year-old man who was admitted 36 hours earlier for symptoms of hyponatraemia and a sodium level of 108 mmol/L(135-145mmol/l) is reviewed. He underwent correction with 1.8% saline. The nurses have noted that he now appears unable to move and they are concerned he is suffering from osmotic demyelination. What is the likely initial cause of osmotic demyelination?
explanation: After rapid correction of low sodium level, loss of cell water, coupled with movement of potassium and sodium into the intracellular space, leads to an increase in intracellular cation concentration that occurs before organic osmolytes are replenished. This leads to protein aggregation and subsequent programmed cell death. Astrocytes are thought to be particularly susceptible to this phenomenon because they express both aquaporin 1 and 4 channels.

stem: A 42-year-old man is found to have multiple peptic ulcers following an episode of upper GI haemorrhage. Investigations reveal a significant elevation in gastrin level. Where is gastrin produced?
options: G cells in the pyloric antrum and duodenum
I cells in the duodenum and jejunum
explanation: G cells in the pyloric antrum and duodenum are responsible for the production of gastrin. The presence of gastrin stimulates parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. Gastrinomas, which are usually benign, produce excessive amounts of gastrin, leading to the development of multiple peptic ulcers, accounting for this patient's presentation. Surgical resection is the intervention of choice for gastrinoma.

stem: A 24-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic. He complains that on the past two visits for holidays in Portugal, he developed diarrhoea. This was self-Limiting and lasted for 72 hours on each occasion. What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are classical for traveller's diarrhoea, which is caused by non-enterotoxin-forming E. coli. Where there are more severe symptoms, these may be due to an enterotoxigenic strain. Symptoms are usually self-Limiting and resolve over a 72-hour period. Taking acid suppressants, such as proton pump inhibitors, may increase the risk of it occurring. Antibiotic treatment is not usually required. Azithromycin may be given as empirical therapy to patients with severe symptoms.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and itching, which have slowly increased in severity over the past four months. She also has vague right upper quadrant discomfort. She has xanthelasma and scratch marks over her upper body and abdomen. There is two-finger breadth hepatomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 104 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.0×109/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 92×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 135 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 85 U/L 1-40 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 385 U/L 30-130 U/L Bilirubin 19 μmol/L 21 μmol/L Which autoantibody is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation: This patient's slowly progressive tiredness and itching, with an obstructive picture on liver function testing, is highly suggestive of primary biliary cholangitis. Around 90-95% of patients with the condition have anti- mitochondrial antibodies, compared to around 0.5% of the general population. Transient elastography is used to determine the degree of liver stiffness associated with the condition and liver biopsy may be considered for staging. Ursodeoxycholic acid may be of value in patients with early-stage disease.

stem: A72-year-old man is reviewed on the ward some 12 hours after returning from haemodialysis. He has a neck line for haemodialysis and is recovering from a myocardial infarction and Gram-negative sepsis. He has developed a fever with a temperature of 38.5℃.His BP is 105/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 102 bpm and regular. There are no focal signs of infection. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 92 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 13.1×10/ 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 180×10/ 150-400×109/ C-reactive protein (CRP) 73 mg/l 10 mg/l What is the most likely cause of this patient's fever?
explanation: S.epidermidis and S. aureus are common causes of indwelling line infection, with S. epidermidis thought to be responsible for around 30% of cases. Given this patient has most likely had his dialysis catheter for a few days and there are no focal signs of infection, S. epidermidis is most likely responsible for his symptoms and raised C-reactive protein level. Vancomycin is a commonly used empirical intervention for sepsis associated with indwelling lines because it has very good coverage against staphylococci. Dosing is based on dry weight at the end of dialysis.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a swelling on the left side of her face. She has Sjogren syndrome. There is a 2-cm smooth swelling at the angle of the left side of the jaw and the orifice of the parotid gland on the left- hand side looks normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Salivary gland stone formation is seen as a rare complication of Sjgren syndrome and accounts for the parotid gland swelling seen here at the angle of the left side of the jaw. Sialography is the investigation of choice to demonstrate any gland obstruction. Conservative management,including measures to increase salivary flow, may be adequate to resolve the problem. Surgical removal of the stone may occasionally be required.

stem: A 49-year-old man who has long-standing type l diabetes is reviewed in the Diabetes Clinic following pan- retinal photocoagulation. What is this patient most likely to complain of?
explanation: Impaired night vision is common in patients who undergo pan-retinal photocoagulation. Loss of peripheral and colour vision is also seen. More worrying signs include eye pain, eye reddening and loss of central vision, especially if this is seen suddenly.

stem: A 49-year-old man who has a history of alcoholism presents to the Dermatology Clinic complaining of a photosensitive erythematous rash with bullae. The lesions heal poorly and his skin is fragile. There is increased pigmentation and hypertrichosis. Which enzyme is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
explanation: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is the enzyme which is deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda(PCT). PCT can be inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, but sporadic cases are much more common, with most related to alcoholism. Itis a cutaneous porphyria where a photosensitive rash develops, as seen here. Use of sun block and avoidance of alcohol are the initial interventions of choice. Venesection may be required where there is iron overload.

stem: A 64-year-old man is commenced on celecoxib for severe arthritic pain affecting his knees, elbows and ankles. He has a previous myocardial infarction and New York Heart Association class Il heart failure. Which side-effect of celecoxib is of most concern here?
explanation: Celecoxib is a selective cyclo-oxygenase 2(COX-2) inhibitor, which is associated with a lower risk of gastrointestinal haemorrhage vs non-selective NSAIDs, although it carries a similar risk of exacerbating cardiac failure. Trials of COX-2 inhibitors also showed that they carry a potentially greater risk of ischaemic cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and stroke. Rather than being associated with cholestatic jaundice, they are predominantly associated with hepatocellular dysfunction.

stem: A 49-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with bilateral knee pain and stiffness. He has diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin and has been told by his General Practitioner that he has abnormal liver function. He appears tanned. There are spider naevi over the upper chest and a 1-cm liver edge on abdominal palpation. Knee flexion is limited bilaterally by pain and stiffness. Knee X-ray shows bilateral chondrocalcinosis. What is the most likely cause of this patient's knee pain?
explanation: This patient's symptoms of diabetes, abnormal liver function and increased pigmentation raise the possibility of hereditary haemochromatosis. Haemochromatosis is associated with pyrophosphate arthropathy, which leads to the chondrocalcinosis seen here. Iron overload and underlying haemochromatosis should be confirmed, with venesection as the intervention of choice. Non-steroidals and colchicine are potential options to treat the joint pain.

stem: A72-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with nausea, vomiting and yellowing of vision, thought to be related to digoxin overdose. Which of the following best fits with the mode of action of digoxin?
explanation: The primary mode of action of digoxin is thought to be via inhibition of the sodium-potassium exchange pump. This leads to an increase in the intracellular sodium level, which, in turn, drives increased activity of the sodium-calcium exchanger and an increase in the intracellular calcium level. This is positively inotropic. Blocking the same exchange pump in the autonomic nervous system drives increased vagal efferent impulses, reduced sympathetic tone and a decreased conduction rate through the atria.

stem: A36-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic for investigation following a fourth second- trimester miscarriage in the last five years. She has intermittent joint pains and suffers from migraines, but is otherwise well. Her BP is 122/72 mmHg and her BMI is 22 kg/m. Investigations: What is the most appropriate next investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 108 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.3×10/L 4-11×10/ Platelets(PLT) 142×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.8 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Antinuclear antibody Positive
explanation: Thrombophilia explanations Thirty per cent of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have positive anti-phospholipid antibodies. They are found in 1-5% of individuals without SLE. There is an increased risk of thromboembolic disease with prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), symptoms including recurrent miscarriage in women and an increased risk of migraine. In the event that the diagnosis is confirmed, then future pregnancies should be managed with low-molecular-weight heparin and aspirin.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with 100-ml haemoptysis. He has been feeling unwell for the past two weeks with a flu-Like illness, which has developed into a nagging cough and shortness of breath. He feels lethargic and nauseated His BP is 155/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 95 bpm and regular. There are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigations Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 91 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 301×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 425μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 9 mm/hour 10 mm/hour What autoantibody is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation: Goodpasture Syndrome explanations This patient has pulmonary haemorrhage with acute renal failure against a background of a normal ESR. This makes anti-glomerular basement membrane(GBM) disease the most likely diagnosis. It is more common in men who smoke. The presence of anti-GBM antibodies confirms the diagnosis. ChestX-ray usually shows patchy shadowing because of the presence of pulmonary haemorrhage. Renal or transbronchial biopsy can be used to obtain a tissue diagnosis. Plasma exchange, coupled with high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide, is the preferred management.

stem: A45-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with right shoulder weakness. He tells you he fell off his bike around two weeks ago in what he thought was a relatively minor fall. Forty-eight hours later, he got excruciating pain in the right shoulder,which was exacerbated by movement and not relieved by paracetamol and ibuprofen. His pain has now subsided, but there is marked weakness of the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, serratus anterior and deltoid muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The sudden onset of severe shoulder pain not relieved by non-opiate analgesics, together with gradual resolution and generalised shoulder weakness as the pain resolves, fits well with a diagnosis of brachial neuritis. The aetiology of brachial neuritis is unknown, although an inherited form is described associated with mutations in the SEPT9 gene. Physiotherapy to maintain the range of movement is the main intervention, followed by strengthening exercises once pain has resolved.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with smalljoint polyarthritis affecting her fingers, wrists, elbows, ankles and feet. Symptoms have lasted for the past eight weeks and have failed to respond adequately to regular naproxen.
