Investigations: Investigation Result Rheumatoid factor Positive Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies Positive What is the most appropriate long-term intervention?
explanation: Methotrexate is the long-term intervention of choice for rheumatoid arthritis. It is given as a once-weekly dose in conjunction with folic acid. It is proven in clinical trials to reduce joint destruction. It is thought to block adenosine signalling in rheumatoid arthritis, thereby downregulating immune cell activity. In patients who fail to achieve control with methotrexate alone, an anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agent, such as infliximab, can be considered.

stem: A39-year-old man is reviewed in the Gastroenterology Clinic after presenting with severe epigastric pain to the Emergency Department. An endoscopy found multiple gastric and duodenal ulcers. Gastrin is significantly elevated. Where is the most likely site of any tumour-producing gastrin?
explanation: Gastrinomas are most commonly found in the pancreas or in the first part of the duodenum. Around 70% are found in the pancreas. High-dose proton pump inhibitors are the initial intervention of choice. Surgical options include partial pancreatectomy and Whipple's procedure and isolated liver metastases may also be resected. Duodenectomy may be considered for tumours within the duodenum. Up to 60% of gastrinomas are thought to have malignant potential.

stem: A38-year-old man who has psoriasis which has not been controlled on a range of therapies is commenced on apremilast. What is the mode of action of apremilast?
explanation: Apremilast is a phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor. Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-4 leads to increased intracellular levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate and a consequent reduction in inflammation. Common side-effects include diarrhoea, nausea and headache, as well as possible intolerance due to gastrointestinal adverse effects. A5-day titration schedule is recommended to achieve a dose of 30 mg twice daily.

stem: A72-year-old man, who is a retired plumber is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough. His General Practitioner prescribed a salbutamol inhaler, but this has had no effect on his symptoms. He smokes 20 cigarettes per day. His BP is 132/82 mmHg and his heart rate is 79 bpm and regular. There is pitting oedema of both ankles. He has inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields on auscultation of the chest. Oxygen saturation is 93% as measured on pulse oximetry. Investigation Result Normal value ChestX-ray Patchy bilateral shadowing and evidence of pleural plaques What intervention is likely to have the greatest impact on prognosis?
explanation: This patient's chest X-ray and clinical findings raise the possibility of underlying asbestosis, given asbestos exposure is the cause of pleural plaques and the symptoms are suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis. Out of the options given, only smoking cessation significantly impacts on life expectancy because it reduces both progression of asbestosis symptoms and the risk of bronchial carcinoma(approximate doubling of risk vs asbestos exposure alone).

stem: A 42-year-old woman with alcoholism is referred to the Maxillofacial Surgeons for teeth removal. She has several loose teeth and evidence of severe gum disease. She also complains of multiple joint pains and on examination, areas of petechial haemorrhage of the skin are noted. What is the most likely vitamin deficiency?
explanation: Vitamin C deficiency fits with the symptoms here, particularly joint pains, petechial haemorrhage and accelerated gum disease. It is seen in alcoholics for a number of reasons, including: self-neglect and inadequate oral intake; chronic diarrhoea and pancreatitis leading to increased faecal loss; and increased urinary excretion of vitamin C due to alcohol excess. Although combination vitamin B replacement is the most important step in treating malnutrition associated with alcoholism, the possibility of coexisting vitamin C deficiency should not be discounted.

stem: A74-year-old man has a combined cardioverter-defibrillator and pacemaker, which was inserted some three years earlier. He is concerned as the device has fired three times in the course of the day. He has been monitored in the Emergency Department and remains in sinus rhythm with occasional paced beats. A decision is made to pass a magnet over the device, as the Cardiac Technician is unavailable for some time. How does the magnet work in this situation?
options: Resets the defibrillator to its last programmed setting
Resets the pacemaker to its last programmed setting
Resets both the defibrillator and the pacemaker to its last programmed setting
Turns off the defibrillator portion of the device
Turns off the pacemaker portion of the device
explanation: Modern implantable defibrillators have a magnet-sensitive switch built in that can turn off the defibrillator portion of the device and switch the pacemaker to an asynchronous pacing mode. This can be useful in an emergency situation when the device is suspected of malfunctioning but a technician who is an expert in programming it is unavailable. In the real world, electromagnetic interference which disrupts the functioning of such devices can occur in airport scanners. Machines which produce a magnetic field within the operating room may also activate the off-switch of the implantable defibrillator.

stem: A 27-year-old man is referred to the Cardiology Clinic with shortness of breath on exercise and central chest pain worse on inspiration. He was unwell a few weeks earlier with a viral respiratory illness. His BP is 112/82 mmHg and his heart rate is 83 bpm and regular. His chest is clear on auscultation. His ECG shows widespread concave ST-segment elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chronic effusive pericarditis is typical of the picture seen here with chest pain and shortness of breath some time after a viral infection, as well as concave ST-segment elevation seen on the ECG. Apart from post-viral pericarditis, effusive pericarditis is also seen in patients with hypothyroidism.Colchicine and non-steroidal anti- inflammatory agents are the mainstay of therapy.

stem: A 24-year-old man is presents to the Emergency Department because he is unable to walk. He is a habitual user of nitrous oxide canisters. Lower limb examination reveals spasticity, clonus and hyperreflexia, with upgoing plantars. What else are you most likely to find?
explanation: Impaired proprioception is a function of posterior column dysfunction which is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency and subacute combined degeneration of the cord, the most likely diagnosis here. Low vitamin B2 levels are increasingly recognised in habitual users of nitrous oxide. Other features of posterior column dysfunction include impairment of fine touch sensation. Cessation of nitrous oxide and vitamin B replacement may be associated with an improvement in symptoms.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department. She felt out of control and that she could not breathe; she had pins and needles in her hands and palpitations and felt light-headed. On admission to the Emergency Department, she has a respiratory rate of 35 breaths/minute, pleuritic chest pain and oxygen saturation of 95% on pulse oximetry. She tells you she had a similar episode five months earlier in a nightclub. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The two discrete episodes of anxiety with palpitations and light-headedness occurring in a stressful environment fit with panic disorder.The pins and needles in the hands are likely a result of a decrease in ionised calcium level related to hyperventilation. Cognitive behavioural therapy(CBT) is the intervention of choice, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors an option in patients who fail to respond to CBT alone.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with dizziness and nausea. She says the episodes of dizziness come on suddenly and last for 20-30 seconds, resolving rapidly if the head is kept still There is no tinnitus. Neurological examination and examination of the external ear and tympanic membrane are unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Hallpike's manoeuvre is the diagnostic test for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo(BPPV) whereby the head is repositioned to reproduce symptoms. A positive result provokes vertigo and rotatory upbeat nystagmus where the upper pole of the eye beats towards the dependent ear, with the vertical component towards the forehead when the patient is looking straight ahead.

stem: A42-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with fever of 38.6℃and rigors over the last 12 hours. Sheis three weeks after her last cycle of chemotherapy for colon cancer. There is no obvious focus of infection on examination. She has an indwelling line for chemotherapy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 2.1×10/L 4-11×109/ Neutrophil count 0.1×10/L 1.5-8.0×109/L Platelets(PLT) 80×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Both S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci are well recognised as common causes of neutropenic sepsis, potentially via infection of an indwelling chemotherapy line. Other common causes include streptococi. enterococci, E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. A broad-spectrum empirical regimen is required initially to cover both Gram-positive and Gram-negative agents-piperacillin/tazobactam and amikacin is a typical regimen.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with disturbance of vision and left-sided eye pain, which has been present for the last 12 hours. She has a left relative afferent pupillary defect and an oedematous left optic disc. What other feature would you expect to find?
options: Severe visual loss with no light perception
explanation: This patient's presentation is typical of acute demyelinating optic neuritis, which is characterised by loss of colour vision, impairment of contrast perception and a relative afferent pupillary defect. The optic disc may appear normal, or it may be oedematous, as seen here. This may be the presenting feature of multiple sclerosis. Use of intravenous corticosteroids can shorten an acute episode of optic neuritis but has not been proven to impact on long-term prognosis.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic for review. He has iron deficiency anaemia and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 4. What is the most likely contributor to this patient's iron deficiency anaemia?
explanation: Hepcidin functions as an acute phase protein and its levels are increased in patients with CKD. It is also a regulator of iron balance. Elevated levels of hepcidin reduce oral iron absorption. Iron is absorbed by the duodenum where it is released into the circulation by ferroportin, to be loaded onto transferrin. Hepcidin induces the degradation of ferroportin and therefore reduces iron absorption. This means that some patients with CKD respond better to intravenous iron replacement.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with extreme lethargy, nausea and swollen ankles. She has been taking regular ibuprofen for the past 2-3 weeks for an ankle injury. Her BP is 155/90 mmHg. She has pitting oedema of both lower limbs. An erythematous rash over her upper body is noted Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/L 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Eosinophils 1.8×10/L 0.05-0.5×10/L Platelets(PLT) 80×10/L 150-400×10/ Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 189μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 24 g/l 35-45 g/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Interstitial Nephritis explanations Acute interstitial nephritis is associated with both use of non-steroidal antibiotics and beta-lactam antibiotics. Features include those seen here with peripheral blood eosinophilia, renal impairment and significant proteinuria. Elevation in immunoglobulin Elevel is also seen. Withdrawal of the causative agent is the most important intervention. High-dose prednisolone may also help accelerate normalisation of renal function.

stem: A32-year-old man visits the Blood Donation Centre wishing to donate blood. Which of the following precludes this patient from donating blood?
options: He is a man who has sex with men
Travelling to Tunisia for a holiday in 2021
explanation: Anyone who has had a blood transfusion or blood products anytime since 1 January 1980 cannot give blood. This is because of the risk of latent Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease where the period of latency and the risk of acquiring the disease through blood transfusion are unknown. Pregnant women, patients who have had an organ transplant and those with previous leukaemia or lymphoma are also unable to donate blood.

stem: A19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with joint pains affecting his left wrist, left ankle, right elbow and right knee. He also has conjunctivitis and pain on passing urine. He had returned from a football team holiday to Spain some two weeks earlier. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 142 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 197×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.2 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 85μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 48 mg/L 10 mg/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Reactive Arthritis Media explanations This patient has oligoarthritis, symptoms of urethritis and conjunctivitis. These symptoms have occurred some two weeks after a trip to Spain and it is possible he may have acquired a sexually transmitted or gastrointestinal infection in that time. Nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea should be considered and antibiotic therapy instituted if it is positive. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) are the first-choice intervention for joint pains and corticosteroids are an option in patients who do not respond to NSAIDs alone.

stem: A 61-year-old man with type ll diabetes has been using a flash glucose monitor at home to learn more about how diet affects his blood glucose levels. He is worried about a peak in his blood glucose levels in the middle of the morning each day. Which of the following foods has the highest glycaemic index?
explanation: White rice is the greatest contributor to glucose load for communities who consume rice as part of their staple diet. The glycaemic index is calculated out of 100, which is the score given to the rise in blood sugar level when glucose itself is ingested. White rice causes approximately 70% of the rise seen for glucose, which gives it a score of 70.Foods with a score of above 70 are rated as having a high glycaemic index.

stem: A40-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department with a photosensitive rash,joint pains, haematuria and proteinuria. She has felt increasingly unwell over the past week. Which of the following is most likely to be found on investigation?
explanation: This patient's presentation is consistent with active lupus where there is also renal involvement. Active lupus causes increased consumption of complement factors that, in turn, leads to low levels of the complement factor C3. Autoantibody screening is likely to reveal positive anti-nuclear antibodies. In this case, given active renal involvement, mycophenolate mofetil is likely to be a better option, compared to hydroxychloroquine which is predominantly used for patients with joint disease.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department having accidentally injected his wife's adrenaline autoinjector into his left thumb some 20 minutes earlier. His thumb is cold and pale and there is no distal capillary refill. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
options: Injection of atropine into the thumb
explanation: Accidental injection of digits with an adrenaline autoinjector is very rare. A number of interventions have been trialled, including a conservative approach with rewarming of the digit only, nitroglycerin paste and phentolamine injected into the same area as where adrenaline was injected. No definitive conclusions can be drawn as to the best intervention, although most expert reviews recommend topical nitroglycerin initially, followed by phentolamine if the patient fails to improve.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is reviewed in the Neurology Clinic, having suffered a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She attends the appointment with her mother who reports she has been generally clumsy in the morning for years, always having sudden jerks of her upper limbs and knocking over things on the breakfast table. Apparently, her mother also suffers from epilepsy, which began in her teenage years. Neurological examination in the clinic is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are suspicious of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy where myoclonic jerks, which are worse in the morning, can pre-date generalised tonic-clonic seizures by a number of years. It is known to carry an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Although sodium valproate is an effective intervention, it is not recommended because of teratogenicity and the fact that use is associated with a polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)-Like syndrome. For this reason, levetiracetam is a commonly used first-line therapy. Alternatives include lamotrigine,although it can slightly worsen the myoclonic episodes.

stem: A 23-year-old man who has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is referred to the Cardiology Clinic because of a heart murmur and intermittent palpitations. His BP is 135/85mmHg. He has a mid-systolic click, followed by a late systolic murmur, loudest at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The murmur here is consistent with mitral valve prolapse. Studies consistently have estimated that 15% of patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease have mitral prolapse, 30% have mitral regurgitation,10-20% have aortic regurgitation and 5% have tricuspid prolapse. Given the history of palpitations, beta blockade may be indicated. Surgical intervention is generally recommended before symptoms of heart failure develop.

stem: A 78-year-old man is recovering from a left hemiarthroplasty undergone two days earlier and is acutely confused. He was previously well and living independently. He has evidence of a left lower lobe pneumonia. He has pulled out his IV line and is trying to bite the nursing staff when they go near him. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Haloperidol is the recommended first-Line pharmaceutical option for treating delirium in the elderly where patients present a risk to themselves or others. Relatively small doses of 0.5-1 mg IM may be sufficient in the first instance to control acute confusion and maintain compliance with clinical care. In patients with significant features of parkinsonism, lorazepam is a more appropriate first-line option because of the risk of worsening any underlying movement disorder.

stem: A 45-year-old man who is HIV-positive presents to the Renal Clinic with pitting oedema affecting both lower limbs. He is poorly compliant with his antiretroviral therapy. His BP is 145/90 mmHg and his BMI is 23 kg/m There is pitting oedema of both lower limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 112 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 5.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 192×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 195μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein 3+, blood negative What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Glomerulonephritis(Nephrotic and Nephritic syndrome) Media explanations This man has deteriorating renal function and proteinuria against a background of poor compliance with antiretroviral therapy.The most likely diagnosis therefore is HIV-associated nephropathy, which has an appearance on renal biopsy similar to that of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Intensification of antiretroviral therapy is the intervention of choice. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors have a potential role to play in reducing progression of renal disease.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with episodes of diarhoea, palpitations and flushing. She has lost 6kg in weight over the past three months. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg and her heart rate is 84 bpm and regular. She has a pansystolic murmur that is loudest in the tricuspid area. Her BMI is 21 kg/m. Investigations: What is the most useful investigation? Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115-155 g/L White cell count(WCC) 8.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 103×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L
explanation: Carcinoid Tumours Media explanations This patient has episodes of flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations, coupled with a murmur suggestive of tricuspid regurgitation. Coupled with anaemia, low PLT count and low K+level, this raises the possibility of carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome is related to excess 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) and 5-HIAA is a metabolite of 5-HT. Somatostatin analogues are indicated to control symptoms.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a cerebral venous thrombosis. She has a family history of an inherited high-affinity haemoglobin (Hb) variant. What is the most likely finding?
explanation: High-affinity Hb variants lead to relative tissue hypoxia because of defective tissue oxygen release. This leads to an increase in haematocrit, which drives up red cell mass and Hb levels. The partial pressure of 50% saturation of Hb(p50) is of key importance in making the diagnosis-levels are low (reference range 24.0-27.0 mmHg). Venesection is the mainstay of therapy for high-affinity Hb variants where there is a significant increase in red cell mass.

stem: A 79-year-old man who lives alone is admitted to the Care of the Elderly Ward with fluctuating confusion. He has been found sleeping by his home help in the middle of the afternoon and seems to be bumping into things on his left-hand side. He is normally independent and goes to the pub each evening. He is drowsy, with a GCS score of 13 and has left-sided sensory inattention and extensive bruising due to frequent falls. What is the most likely cause of this patient's confusion?
explanation: In this patient who may well have a problem with excess alcohol consumption, with evidence of bruising from falls, a subdural haematoma is the main diagnosis to exclude. It fits with the transient confusion and the left- sided sensory inattention, indicating possible right-sided haemorrhage. Head CT is the most appropriate next step, with review by Neurosurgery to determine if evacuation of any clot is appropriate.

stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the Medical Admissions Ward with a new ejection systolic murmur,fever and weight loss over the last three months. He recently had a number of teeth extracted. His temperature is 37.7 ℃, his BP is 135/82mmHg and his heart rate is 75 bpm and irregular. There is an ejection systolic murmur, loudest in the aortic area. There are splinter haemorrhages affecting the fingernails of both hands. What finding is most suggestive of bacterial endocarditis?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are suspicious of bacterial endocarditis following his recent dental work and the systolic murmur with the presence of splinter haemorrhages is also suggestive of the diagnosis. It is fever, however, that forms part of the minor Dukes'criteria for endocarditis. Other minor criteria include: · a predisposing heart condition or intravenous drug use · vascular phenomena · immunological phenomena ·microbiological evidence(but not fitting the major criterion of two positive blood cultures with a typical organism found).

stem: A 24-year-old woman who has recently been dealing with the death of her father from a stroke complains of weakness of her left leg. She says that her left leg is numb and she is unable to weight-bear. Examination reveals normal tone and reflexes. When you lift up her leftleg, she appears to slowly lower it to the ground rather than it dropping suddenly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Conversion disorder is characterised by a presentation with unexplained significant neurological symptoms. These can include loss of vision, deafness and weakness of an arm or leg. The symptoms develop in response to a stressful situation such as this patient's recent bereavement. The fact she lowers her leg slowly to the ground fits with a functional disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 19-year-old man requests human papillomavirus (HPV) vacination because he has heard that it protects against HPV16, which causes other cancers, apart from cervical cancer. What other cancer is most strongly associated with HPV16?
explanation: As well as being associated with cervical cancer, HPV16 is also associated with oropharyngeal and anal cancers and with penile cancer in men. Prophylactic vaccination has been shown to reduce the rate of oral and oropharyngeal HPV infection by around 80% and this would be expected to translate into a reduced incidence of cancer over time.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe spasm of the neck and a fixed gaze. She can only look to the left. Her neck is twisted and she is unable to straighten it. She was given some metoclopramide by a friend for nausea and vomiting. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has an oculogyric crisis, which can be precipitated by drugs with dopamine agonist properties, including metoclopramide. It is characterised by neck spasm and a fixed gaze. Acute interventions can include anticholinergic agents or antihistamines. Standard doses are 2 mg of benztropine, 5 mg of procyclidine or 50 mg of diphenhydramine. Neurological adverse events associated with treatment have discouraged the use of metoclopramide, particularly in young women and the elderly.

stem: A 65-year-old man, who has chronic kidney disease, is referred to the Emergency Department because a routine blood test at his General Practice Surgery has revealed a potassium level of 6.4 mmol/l(3.5-5.2 mmol/L). An urgent ECG is arranged on arrival in the department. What feature on the ECG signifies the highest risk of cardiac arrest?
explanation: QT prolongation is seen in severe hyperkalaemia where potassium levels are generally above 7.0 mmol/L. It is an indicator of an imminent cardiac arrest. The initial intervention should be to gain IV access and deliver IV calcium chloride under cardiac monitoring. This is followed by treatment to reduce the potassium level acutely, usually with a glucose-and-insulin infusion, which can be used to buy time, while the cause of hyperkalaemia is investigated.

stem: A52-year-old man has an erythematous rash affecting both cheeks with telangiectasiae. His nose is also erythematous with a number of papules, particularly affecting the nasolabial folds. His skin is quite dry. The rash has failed to respond to topical metronidazole and topical azelaic acid. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has rosacea that has failed to respond to two topical therapies. Oral intervention is the next logical step, with doxycycline supported by a Cochrane meta-analysis of rosacea treatments. A dose of 40 mg once daily is usually prescribed. For patients who cannot take tetracycline antibiotics, erythromycin is a potential alternative. Isotretinoin is an option for patients with disease resistant to antibiotics.

stem: A 34-year-old man with psoriasis for the past four years presents to the clinic with arthritis which has led to a sausage-like appearance affecting three fingers on each hand. He takes regular naproxen and weekly methotrexate, but feels his arthritis is steadily getting worse. Which human leukocyte antigen type is most associated with psoriasis?
explanation: Human leukocyte antigen-B27 is associated with psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and arthritis associated with Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 38-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department from a paracetamol overdose. He has recently lost his job and thinks he is unable to pay his mortgage. He is referred to the Psychiatric Liaison Social Worker Which of the following factors would be associated with an increased suicide risk?
options: Access to the Community Psychiatric Nurse
Having two children aged under 10 years
Regular contact with his best friend
explanation: Alcohol and substance abuse is recognised as a risk factor for completed suicide because it is associated with impulsive behaviour. Other individual risk factors include: · A history of depression or other mental illnesses Q. Answered Flagged ·chronic pain or other long-term disability · criminal record · job loss · impulsive or aggressive tendencies · adverse childhood experiences · sense of hopelessness · victim or perpetrator of violence.

stem: A 40-year-old man comes to the clinic for review of his asthma. His current therapy is inhaled beclomethasone 200 μg twice daily. Symptoms are much worse at night when he wakes 2-3 times because of coughing. He takes over-the-counter omeprazole for symptoms of reflux oesophagitis. His chest is clear on auscultation. His peak flow is 500 litres/min (620 predicted). His BMl is 35 kg/m. What is the most appropriate next step in therapy?
explanation: This patient has predominantly nocturnal asthma symptoms that are not completely resolved by inhaled corticosteroids. Given he also has gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms, a trial of regular omeprazole is most appropriate. A twice-daily omeprazole regimen is usually prescribed. Trials of proton pump inhibitors have not consistently shown improvement in respiratory function, although a high level of response with respect to asthma symptom scores is reported in patients with predominantly nocturnal coughing and shortness of breath.

stem: Infection control measures are required for one of the Elderly Care Wards because of an outbreak of Clostridium difficile. What is the most important method to reduce the spread of C. difficile?
options: Disinfection of rooms where a patient with C.difficile has been cared for
explanation: C.difficile is resistant to alcohol hand rub, meaning this is not an option to prevent the spread of C. difficile infection. The only option is washing with soap and water. This is usually complemented with use of gloves and apron when providing care for a patient with C.difficile. The treatment of choice is oral vancomycin, which achieves a high intraluminal concentration within the bowel and is thought to be more effective than metronidazole in clearing the bacterium.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department. She has had a call from her sister to say that her niece has developed chickenpox and she saw the child the previous day. She is 12 weeks pregnant with her first child and cannot remember having had chickenpox herself. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Testing for varicella-zoster immunoglobulin G(IgG) antibodies is the crucial first step in assessing this patient. In the event they are positive, then no further intervention is needed. If they are negative, then varicella-zoster immune globulin(VZIG) should be given. When patients present with chickenpox symptoms, they should be given aciclovir if they are within the first 24 hours of onset.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for follow-up after his latest colonoscopy. He has familial adenomatous polyposis with an identified APC mutation. His colonoscopy has shown20 polyps, some with high-grade dysplasia. What is the most appropriate plan for this patient's treatment?
options: Proctocolectomy with stapled ileal pouch-anal anastomosis
explanation: lleal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) is the intervention of choice in this patient who has a significant risk of progression to colon cancer, given the number of polyps found and the fact that some show high-grade dysplasia. Out of the options given, proctocolectomy allows for removal of as much potentially cancerous mucosa as possible. It is still possible to develop cancer in the anal transition zone and removal of the anal mucosa can further reduce the chance of developing cancer.

stem: A 24-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency department with a hives-like rash, stridor and tongue swelling. He has been walking in the countryside when he suddenly fellilL. His BP is 90/50 mmHg and his heart rate is 125 bpm and regular. He is treated with fluid loading,hydrocortisone and IM adrenaline. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient has suffered suspected anaphylaxis which may have occurred due to a wasp or bee sting, given he was walking in the countryside. Elevated tryptase levels are highly suspicious of anaphylaxis and measurement is recommended as soon as possible after emergency treatment has been instigated, preferably within 1-2 hours. A further sample can be taken after 24 hours or at the ALlergy Clinic. The normal range is 2- 14μg/L. Sensitivity to wasp or bee venom can be tested for by radioallergosorbent testing(RAST)(which measures allergy-specific immunoglobulin E).Assuming the diagnosis is confirmed, he may be advised to carry an adrenaline pen in future.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain, distension and confusion. Her BP is 95/60 mmHg and her heart rate is 132 bpm and irregular. Her abdomen is distended and painful and she has quiet bowel sounds. Lactate is significantly elevated at 4.9mmol/L(0.5-2.2 mmol/). Where is the lesion causing this patient's symptoms most likely to be found?
explanation: The splenic flexure is a watershed area which receives blood supply from terminal branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. This makes it particularly vulnerable to ischaemic colitis, which fits with the presentation here with abdominal pain, distension and a significant elevation in lactate level.CT angiography is the investigation of choice for mesenteric ischaemia, with surgical intervention as the definitive option, although many patients either present too late for surgery or are unfit for surgical intervention due to co- morbidities.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is started on olanzapine for treatment of schizophrenia. She asks about potential adverse effects of treatment. Which of the following is the most frequent side-effect of olanzapine?
explanation: Weight gain is very common in association with olanzapine therapy, meaning that it occurs in10% of patients treated with the drug. In between 1% and 10%, this can be associated with features of the metabolic syndrome, including raised blood glucose levels. Uncommonly, the development of diabetes may progress further to an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis.

stem: A34-year-old man is referred to the clinic with severe tiredness and erectile dysfunction over the past few months. His BP is 122/80 mmHg,with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. He looks pale. Bitemporal hemianopia on visual field testing is noted. What is the most appropriate intervention? Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 131 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 5.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.3 mU/L 0.4-4.5 mU/L (TSH) Prolactin 1500 mlU/L 700 mlU/L MRI of the brain 2-cm pituitary adenoma with optic chiasm pressure
explanation: This patient has symptoms of multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies, with biochemistry results consistent with cortisol deficiency, a TSH level which is below the lower limit of the normal range and an elevated prolactin level. Given the size of the tumour, if this were a prolactinoma, a much higher increase in serum prolactin levels would be expected. A non-functioning adenoma is most likely,meaning that surgical resection is the most practical option.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who works in a children's day care unit presents to the Emergency Department complaining of anal itching, particularly at night andsaid she found something wriggling that looked like a piece of cotton when she wiped on one occasion in the last week. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: E. vermicularis is the commonest helminth infection seen in the UK, causing a condition known as threadworm or pinworm infection. It presents, as in this patient, with symptoms of anal itching, predominantly at night and the presence of small cotton-like worms, as seen here, when the patient wipes or on the underwear, particularly overnight. Mebendazole is the intervention of choice in adults and children over the age of two years.

stem: A 61-year-old woman, who has type ll diabetes, cardiovascular disease and hypertension, presents to the Emergency Department. She started with symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection a few days ago but is now extremely worried as she has developed a number of severe ulcers in her mouth, as well as generalised target lesions, some of which have become necrotic. She also has conjunctivitis. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation: Indapamide contains a sulfonamide moiety, which significantly increases the risk of Steven-Johnson syndrome (the cause of this patient's skin rash). Other drugs known to cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome include allopurinol, carbamazepine,trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, abacavir, phenytoin, sodium valproate and lamotrigine. Withdrawal of indapamide is a crucial first step in treatment. Therapy is supportive with fluid replacement, analgesia and prevention of secondary infection.

stem: A 25-year-old man has developed an ulcerated lesion on his left shin. He says it began as a small papule but grew rapidly. It is now 4cm across and has a necrotic centre surrounded by small abscesses and a raised edge. He has ulcerative colitis which is controlled by regular mesalamine. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are useful to halt progression of pyoderma gangrenosum(the diagnosis here) and prevent the appearance of new lesions. High doses(60 mg daily) are often required and pulsed methylprednisolone can be used as an alternative. Topical high-potency steroids such as triamcinolone may also be of value. Steroid-sparing agents include ciclosporin, azathioprine and anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) therapies.

stem: A 74-year-old man is reviewed on the Elderly Care Ward. He has end-stage bronchial carcinoma and is expected to die within a few hours. He is unconscious. His relatives are concerned because he has excess respiratory secretions, which are precipitating bouts of coughing, during which he appears to moan and be agitated. What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Hyoscine is an anticholinergic agent that can be given subcutaneously to control excess respiratory secretions in the terminal phase of life. Both hyoscine hydrobromide and hyoscine butylbromide can be repeated every 4- 6 hours. Glycopyrronium is a potential alternative to hyoscine and studies suggest there is little difference in efficacy between the two.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department complaining of being tired all the time, double vision at the end of the day and problems keeping her eyes open past 21:00 in the evening. On examination, she has fatigable ptosis. A chestX-ray shows a smooth mass in the upper half of the chest, near the junction of the heart and great vessels. What is the most likely cause of this patient's abnormal chest X-ray?
options: Small cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus
explanation: This patient's symptoms are suspicious of myasthenia gravis. Around 15% of patients with myasthenia gravis have a thymoma and around 30-50% of patients with a thymoma have myasthenia gravis. Early symptoms are typical of those seen here with generalised lethargy, double vision and fatigable ptosis. Diagnosis is based on the presence of autoantibodies, including anti-acetylcholine receptor, anti-MuSK or anti-LRP4, electrophysiology studies and response to cholinesterase inhibitors. Immunosuppression is also of value to limit progression of weakness.

stem: A 42-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with shortness of breath on exercise. He is a non- smoker and has no significant past medical history. Auscultation of the chest is normal. His BMI is 35 kg/m Which is the most likely abnormal test?
options: Forced expiratory volume in one second
explanation: Expiratory reserve volume the extra volume of air that can be expelled with forced effort vs a standard respiration, is significantly reduced, even in moderate obesity. It is also impacted by weight loss where significant improvements are seen after weight loss surgery. An increased prevalence of asthma is seen in obese patients, although it is unclear whether this is due to increased airway hyperreactivity or due to increased inflammation.

stem: A 49-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with symptoms of severe anaemia. He carries a card with him stating that he must receive irradiated blood in the event of a transfusion. What is the reason for transfusing only irradiated blood?
explanation: The main reason for using irradiated blood is to prevent the occurrence of graft-versus-host disease when donor white cells in the transfused unit attack host tissues, including the skin, GI tract and bone marrow in particular. Patients particularly at risk who should receive irradiated blood include those with: · Hodgkin's lymphoma.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has suffered bilateral lens dislocations and a right shoulder dislocation presents to the Emergency Department with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. There is a 20-mmHg difference in systolic BP between the arms. His ECG shows inferolateral T-wave inversion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This man's history of lens dislocation and shoulder dislocation fits with possible Marfan syndrome in which aortic dissection is recognised to occur. It is associated with sudden-onset tearing chest pain which radiates to the back and as here, a differential in BP between the two arms is often seen. Transthoracic ECHO is a useful initial bedside test to confirm the diagnosis and MRI is the optimal way to confirm the aortic architecture, prognosis and the need for surgical intervention. Q.
